title: CDN & Live Streaming
description: Master CDN origin-to-edge architecture, cache warming strategies, RTMP ingest, low-latency HLS, WebRTC for sub-second streaming, and Netflix Open Connect.

segments.text: Netflix streams over seventeen percent of all downstream internet traffic globally. Serving this from a single data center is physically impossible — light takes sixty-eight milliseconds to cross the Atlantic. CDNs place content at the edge, close to viewers. The difference: two hundred milliseconds buffering time versus five seconds.

Origin-to-edge architecture: your origin server has all content. Edge servers cache popular content in a hundred-plus locations worldwide. A viewer in Mumbai requests a video — DNS routes them to the nearest edge. Cache hit? Stream directly. Cache miss? Edge fetches from a regional mid-tier cache, then origin if needed. This hierarchy reduces origin load by over ninety-nine percent.

For viral content — a new movie premiere — you can't wait for the first viewer to trigger a cache miss. Cache warming pre-pushes content to edge servers before demand hits. Netflix pre-positions new releases on Open Connect appliances during off-peak hours. When the content goes live, it's already on the edge servers nearest to predicted viewer clusters.

Live streaming starts with RTMP ingest. The streamer's software — OBS, for example — sends an RTMP stream to your ingest server. The ingest server transcodes it into multiple bitrates in real-time and segments it into two to six second HLS chunks. These chunks are distributed to edge servers within seconds of being created.

Streaming latency is a spectrum. Traditional HLS: fifteen to thirty seconds latency, great reliability. Low-Latency HLS with partial segments: two to four seconds, good for sports. WebRTC: sub-second, real-time interaction possible. Each step toward lower latency sacrifices buffering resilience. Choose based on your use case — live auctions need WebRTC, movie streaming needs HLS.

You're designing a live sports streaming service for the World Cup final — expected peak of three hundred million concurrent viewers. What's your CDN architecture, and how do you handle the thundering herd problem at kickoff?
segments.thought_prompt: Design CDN architecture for 300M concurrent live viewers with thundering herd at kickoff.

segments.text: Low-Latency HLS works by sending partial segments — fragments of a segment before the full segment is complete. Instead of waiting six seconds for a full segment, the player receives one-second partial segments. Combined with blocking playlist reload — the player's request blocks on the server until a new segment is ready — this achieves two to four second glass-to-glass latency.

WebRTC achieves sub-second latency through peer-to-peer connections and UDP transport. No buffering, no segmenting. But it doesn't scale to millions — each viewer needs a direct connection. For broadcast-scale WebRTC, use a Selective Forwarding Unit that receives one stream and forwards it to viewers without transcoding. Twitch experimented with this for interactive streaming.

Netflix Open Connect is a custom CDN. Netflix places hardware appliances inside ISP networks — over eighteen thousand servers in one hundred and sixty countries. Each appliance stores the most popular content for that ISP's subscribers. During peak hours, ninety-five percent of Netflix traffic never leaves the ISP's network. This is why Netflix can deliver four-K reliably.

You're building a video platform that needs both on-demand and live streaming. On-demand needs global reach, live needs low latency. How do you architect a unified CDN strategy that serves both use cases efficiently?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a unified CDN architecture for both on-demand (global reach) and live (low latency) video.

segments.text: Video delivery is a hierarchy of caches from origin to edge. CDN architecture choices depend on your latency requirements: HLS for reliability, LL-HLS for sports, WebRTC for real-time interaction. Cache warming handles predictable demand spikes, and custom CDN appliances like Netflix Open Connect optimize the last mile. The CDN is where video streaming engineering really lives.
